Variation: In 2022/23, there was a total sum of 95 Councillors attendances at 12 Council meetings. In comparison, in 2021/22 there were 100 Councillor attendances at 12 Council meetings.

Description: Cost of elected representation
Variation: The cost of Council elected representatives per Councillor increased by 14.55% from the previous financial year. Influencing factors being, increase to legislated allowances, training/conference costs and associated costs for the Mayors vehicle.

Description: Satisfaction with council decisions
Variation: Bass Coast Council community satisfaction rating for making decisions in the interest of the community decreased by five points from the previous year. The Local Government sector universally experienced a downward trend in community satisfaction levels.

Description: Physical library collection usage
Variation: The number of physical library collection loans increased from 155,928 in 2021/22 to 171,701 in 2022/23.

Description: Recently purchased library collection
Variation: There were 48,836 items in the library collection including e-resources. The number of items purchased in the last 5 years has reduced from 32,452 in 2021/22 to 29,975 in 2022/23.

Description: Active library borrowers in municipality
Variation: There was an increase in active library borrowers from 6,315 in 2021/22 to 6,559 in 2022/23. During this period the municipal population has increased from 40,641 to 41,741 resulting in a 1.63 per cent decrease in active library borrowers compared to municipal population.

Description: Cost of library service per population
Variation: The cost of the library service increased by 3% from 2021/22. During this period the Bass Coast population increased from 40,641 to 41,741 resulting in a minor increase in costs per population.

Description: Infant enrolments in the MCH service
Variation: Council does not have operational control of a MCH Service

Description: Cost of the MCH service
Variation: Council does not have operational control of a MCH Service

Description: Participation in the MCH service
Variation: Council does not have operational control of a MCH Service

Description: Participation in the MCH service by Aboriginal children
Variation: Council does not have operational control of a MCH Service

Description: Participation in 4-week Key Age and Stage visit
Variation: Council does not have operational control of a MCH Service

Description: Sealed local road requests
Variation: Council maintains 602 kilometres of sealed local roads. We received a total of 81 sealed local road requests in 2022/23 compared to 100 requests in 2021/22.

Description: Sealed local roads maintained to condition standards
Variation: In 2022/23 there were 602 kilometres of sealed local roads with 590 kilometres below Councils intervention level. For 2021/22 there were 596 kilometres of sealed local roads with 573 kilometres below Councils intervention level.

Description: Cost of sealed local road reconstruction
Variation: Council's pavement reconstruction costs have decreased per square metre from $113.34 to $111.64 due to an increased proportion of rural road reconstruction from the previous year.

Description: Cost of sealed local road resealing
Variation: In 2022/23 Council resealed 69,830 square metres of sealed local roads compared to 55,422 square metres in 2021/22. There has been a decrease in the cost per square metre from $15.51 in 2021/22 to $12.73 in 2022/23.

Description: Satisfaction with sealed local roads
Variation: Our 2022/23 Community Satisfaction score of 51 is a three point decrease on last years result. Our score is eleven points higher than the average for Large Rural Councils and three points higher than the State-wide average. It is important to note that the survey results are also a reflection of the state controlled roads within the municipality.

Description: Time taken to decide planning applications
Variation: Council has implemented a new software system. The transition has impacted the ability to accurately report for 2022/23.

Description: Planning applications decided within required time frames
Variation: Council has implemented a new software system. The transition has impacted the ability to accurately report for 2022/23.

Description: Cost of statutory planning service
Variation: A 37.91% increase in the direct cost of the statutory planning service compared to the previous year is due to an increase of complex applications requiring legal and consultative services and a decrease in applications received.

Description: Council planning decisions upheld at VCAT
Variation: Of the 495 planning applications determined in 2022/23, there were sixteen VCAT decisions. Five set aside Council's decision whilst the other eleven upheld Council's decision.

Description: Kerbside bin collection requests
Variation: Council serviced 28,747 kerbside collection properties and received 1582 Customer Requests for 2022/23 compared to 1,305 for 2021/22.

Description: Kerbside collection bins missed
Variation: The decrease in performance for missed bins reported, is a result of inclusion of organics bins in the calculation.

Description: Cost of kerbside garbage bin collection service
Variation: The increase in cost of kerbside garbage is primarily due to inflationary pressures within the third party kerbside collection contract.

Description: Cost of kerbside recyclables collection service
Variation: The increase in cost of kerbside recycling is primarily due to inflationary pressures within the third party kerbside collection contract.

Description: Kerbside collection waste diverted from landfill
Variation: The 1.65% increase in Bass Coast Shire Council's diversion rate is due to a reduction in tonnage of kerbside waste collected, this is offset by a smaller decrease in recyclables and organics collected.

Description: Expenses per property assessment
Variation: The 2.9 per cent increase is reflective of a rise in CPI (currently 6 per cent). Waste related expenditure has mostly driven this increase in total expenditure.

Description: Average rate per property assessment
Variation: The 2.14 per cent increase in average rates per property assessment reflects a combination of the 1.75 per cent rate cap and the development of vacant land and existing properties.

Description: Current assets compared to current liabilities
Variation: This indicator has been impacted by a reduction in cash balances and deferred income as a result of capital works delivery. Current liabilities have reduced due to early repayment of borrowings. The 2023/24 forecast increase is due to a short term redraw being refinanced long-term.

Description: Unrestricted cash compared to current liabilities
Variation: The increase in this indicator in 2022/23 is due to a lower value of dedicated cash reserves set aside for completion of carried forward capital works.

Description: Loans and borrowings compared to rates
Variation: During 2022/23 Council drew down on borrowings for construction of intergenerational projects, which will continue during the forward outlook.

Description: Loans and borrowings repayments compared to rates
Variation: A short-term loan rollover ($11.7 million) has been accounted for as a repayment and redraw in each financial year. In 2022/23 this redraw was reduced to $8m, with future year end predictions based on extended loan terms.

Description: Non-current liabilities compared to own source revenue
Variation: The increase in this indicator in 2022/23 and onward is due to the planned draw down of borrowings which will fund the delivery of intergenerational projects.

Description: Asset renewal and upgrade compared to depreciation
Variation: Council has accelerated its capital works delivery and is now renewing and upgrading its assets in line with its asset management plans.

Description: Adjusted underlying surplus (or deficit)
Variation: Council’s underlying result has been impacted by a write off of $2.8 million in road assets and land improvement assets that have been renewed or upgraded.

Description: Rates compared to adjusted underlying revenue
Variation: Council continues to have a reliance on rate revenue consistent with other large rural Council’s.

Description: Rates compared to property values
Variation: The decrease experienced in 2022/23 is due to an average 8 per cent increase in capital improved property values within the municipality.

Description: Expenses per head of municipal population
Variation: The 2022/23 increase of 1.4 per cent is attributable to expense increases in waste kerbside collection contract costs and insurance premiums. The increase in 2020/21 was due to Council’s participation in the Working for Victoria initiative, which while fully funded by the State Government resulted in higher employee expenses.

Description: Infrastructure per head of municipal population
Variation: The value of Council’s infrastructure has increased in 2022/23 as a result of Capital works expenditure ($46 million), independent fair value revaluations ($43 million) and developer contributed assets ($15 million). The 2020/21 increase is due to a fair value adjustment to drainage assets.

Description: Population density per length of road
Variation: The continuous increase in population has resulted in higher density per length of road.

Description: Own-source revenue per head of municipal population
Variation: The 2022/23 increase is due to additional revenue associated with waste user fees and interest earnt on investments. The 2020/21 increase was due to recognition of additional rates and charges revenue raised through the Pioneer Bay special charge scheme.

Description: Recurrent grants per head of municipal population
Variation: Increase in recurrent grants in 2021/22 and 2022/23 is due to increased Victorian Grants Commission funding received in advance. Recurrent Grants received by Council reduced in 20/21 due to the cessation of Aged & Disability services, from January 2020.

Description: Relative Socio-Economic Disadvantage
Variation: The socio-economic disadvantage index is prepared by the ABS. The result has increased from three to five for Bass Coast, on a scale of one for most disadvantaged and ten for least disadvantaged.

Description: Percentage of staff turnover
Variation: Staff turnover in 2022/23 was consistent with 2021/22 and is on par with the industry average. The substantial value in 2019/20 was due to Council decision to cease the provision of Aged Care Services from January 2020.

Description: Health inspections of aquatic facilities
Variation: Council Officers completed inspections of all Council owned aquatic facilities.

Description: Utilisation of aquatic facilities
Variation:
In total, there were 417,261 visits to Council aquatic facilities in 2022/23. 

 

Visits increased by over 65 per cent compared to pre-COVID-19 average attendance, this was largely a result of increased participation and attendance to the basketball stadium which is co-located at this facility.

Description: Cost of aquatic facilities
Variation: Increased attendance at aquatic facilities resulted in a decreased cost per visit.

Description: Time taken to action animal management requests
Variation: Council implemented many processes in the last year to reduce the time taken to action animal management requests. Including additional animal handling training for staff, the use of technology for cat trap hire as well as the provision of more cat traps.

Description: Animals reclaimed
Variation: Council delivered a responsible pet ownership campaign with the aim of reuniting collected animals with their owners. The education program led to the number of animals reclaimed increasing from 284 (last year) to 364 for this year.

Description: Animals rehomed
Variation: Although the number of animals rehomed was less than the previous year, the total percentage of animals either reclaimed or rehomed this year was 94 per cent.

Description: Cost of animal management service per population
Variation:
The cost of animal management service includes costs such as compliance activities, management of the Municipal Animal Pound and veterinary services.

This year's cost is higher than previous years as they incorrectly didn't include compliance related activities. The results for previous years have been restated using the correct formula in Council's Annual Report.

Description: Animal management prosecutions
Variation:
There were five animal management prosecutions, all were successfully pursued by Council.  

Prosecutions are conducted on an as needs basis or when required under the Domestic Animals Act 1994. Council’s primary strategy remains focused on community safety, communication, education, and promotion of responsible pet ownership.

Description: Time taken to action food complaints
Variation: Consistent with previous years, most complaints were responded to within 24 hours. Council responded to 33 complaints in 2022/23.

Description: Food safety assessments
Variation:
Council aims to complete all required annual food safety assessments for registered Class 1 and 2 food premises. 

Food safety assessments have returned to pre-COVID-19 levels. Council completed 392 assessments this year.

Description: Cost of food safety service
Variation: The cost of the Food Safety Service increased on the previous year due to a staff vacancy being filled.

Description: Critical and major non-compliance outcome notifications
Variation: During the year, there were a total of 28 critical and major non-compliance notifications, all of which were followed up by Council.

Description: Council decisions made at meetings closed to the public
Variation:
Due to the commercial nature of decisions relating to tender recommendations and acquisitions, they are considered to be confidential information under the Local Government Act 2020.

The higher result this year was influenced by a number of commercial in confidence waste services related tender recommendations being considered by Council.

Description: Satisfaction with community consultation and engagement
Variation: Satisfaction with consultation and engagement decreased compared to the previous year. The average result for similarly sized Councils was 47.

Description: Councillor attendance at council meetings
Variation: There were 23 Council Meetings in 2022/23. Councillor attendance for the year equated to over 92 per cent.

Description: Cost of elected representation
Variation: The cost of elected representation includes Councillor allowances, the cost of travel to meetings to advocate to State and Federal Governments, the cost of mandatory Councillor Induction, the cost of training, professional development, catering, and IT expenses.

Description: Satisfaction with council decisions
Variation: Satisfaction with Council making decisions in the interest of the community decreased by four points compared to the previous year. The average result for similarly sized Councils was 48.

Description: Physical library collection usage
Variation:
Over 200,000 physical item loans were made during the year, equivalent to 4.38 loans per item. 

The loan of physical library collection items has returned to pre-COVID-19 levels.

Description: Recently purchased library collection
Variation:
There were 57,667 items in the library collection (including e-resources) with 38,670 items being purchased in the last five years. 

The proportion of the library collection that is less than five years old was consistent with previous years.

Description: Active library borrowers in municipality
Variation:
Baw Baw Shire population continues to grow faster than the number of active library borrowers, causing a decrease in this measure.

The average number of active borrowers over the last three years was 6,500.

Description: Cost of library service per population
Variation: A small decrease in the cost of providing the service combined with an increase in population means that the cost per resident has decreased by eight per cent on the previous year.

Description: Infant enrolments in the MCH service
Variation:
All birth notifications received were actioned and all newborns were enrolled in Council’s Maternal and Child Health service. During the year, 655 infants were enrolled in the service.

The result is more than 100 per cent because babies born late in the 2021/22 year participated in the service this financial year.

Description: Cost of the MCH service
Variation:
Council provided over 15,000 hours of Maternal and Child Health Services for families during the year, resulting in a cost of $90.87 per hour of service. 

The increased cost on the previous year is attributed to the spike in births during the COVID-19 financial years (21 per cent above pre-COVID-19 average).

Description: Participation in the MCH service
Variation: The 2022/23 financial year demonstrated an overall participation rate of 69 per cent in the Maternal and Child Health Service. This percentage is marginally lower than the previous financial year as the service continues to be impacted by COVID-19 and other viral illnesses.

Description: Participation in the MCH service by Aboriginal children
Variation: Participation in the Maternal and Child Health service by Aboriginal children was close to 71 per cent and is consistent with previous years.

Description: Participation in 4-week Key Age and Stage visit
Variation: The service received 649 birth notices during the year and conducted 630 four-week Key Age and Stage assessments. Despite the impact of COVID-19, this is a high result and is consistent with previous years.

Description: Sealed local road requests
Variation: Higher than average rainfall increased the number of customer requests received over the year.

Description: Sealed local roads maintained to condition standards
Variation: Council continued to maintain a high proportion of its road network to the condition standards. The condition of the sealed local road network is assessed every four years.

Description: Cost of sealed local road reconstruction
Variation: The cost for 2022/23 was consistent with previous years, noting that last year was higher than usual due to the reconstruction and renewal of a road with a concrete pavement.

Description: Cost of sealed local road resealing
Variation: The increased cost this year was associated with allocating more money on preparation works to increase the longevity of resealing activities.

Description: Satisfaction with sealed local roads
Variation: Satisfaction with sealed local roads decreased by five points compared to the previous year, as did the Statewide and Large Rural Council averages.

Description: Time taken to decide planning applications
Variation:
The high growth rate in Baw Baw and fluctuating workforce in the Planning Department have resulted in a significant backlog of older planning applications.

Determining applications with longer processing dates (which was required to reduce the backlog), caused the median time taken to increase. This year’s higher result is a reflection that Council's Planning Department have made significant progress to work through the applications backlog whilst continuing to stabilise its workforce.

Focusing on reducing the backlog in the first half of the year caused higher results over the whole year. A reduction in processing time (down to 104 days) towards the end of the reporting period demonstrates a significant improvement in performance.

Description: Planning applications decided within required time frames
Variation:
The lower result is due to Council's planning department working through the backlog of historic applications.

The result in the final quarter of the year was 64 per cent, indicating significant improvement compared to earlier in the year and other previous years.

Description: Cost of statutory planning service
Variation:
The increase in cost resulted from the use of contractors both to reduce the backlog of planning applications and to maintain required levels of staffing in an increasingly competitive employment market.

Additional legal advice and/or representation was required for backlog applications, also contributing to the higher cost for this year.

Description: Council planning decisions upheld at VCAT
Variation:
Sixteen of the 25 planning decisions appealed at VCAT were not set aside.

Of the nine decisions that were set aside, seven resulted from a failure to determine (two of which were determined by consent order), one was recommended for refusal, and one required the removal of a condition relating to public open space.

Description: Kerbside bin collection requests
Variation:
Council received approximately 116 bin collection requests per 1,000 residential households, seven less than last year's result.

The requests related to: additional bins, replacement of damaged bins, and missed collections or stolen bins.

Description: Kerbside collection bins missed
Variation:
There was a total of 266 kerbside collection bins missed, or 1.36 for every 10,000 scheduled kerbside garbage and recycling bin lifts. 

This is a reduction of 30 per cent compared to the previous year, despite an increase in the total number of bins collected for the year.

Description: Cost of kerbside garbage bin collection service
Variation: The cost of the kerbside garbage collection equated to $157 per garbage bin. Increasing this year due to the landfill levy, CPI (Consumer Price Index), labour, fuel, and transportation costs.

Description: Cost of kerbside recyclables collection service
Variation: Although total cost of the recycling service increased marginally, an increase in the number of collection bins resulted in a slight reduction to the cost per bin.

Description: Kerbside collection waste diverted from landfill
Variation: The landfill diversion rate for 2022/23 remained consistent with previous years. More than half of the waste collected was recycled or processed for green organics.

Description: Expenses per property assessment
Variation: Council's expense per assessment is in line with prior years. 2021/22 experienced a transfer of $12 million worth of expenditure from capital to operating as the expenditure did not meet the asset threshold. This resulted in an increase in expense per assessment in 2021/22. Expenditure is forecast to return to average levels in future years.

Description: Average rate per property assessment
Variation:
The average rate payable for each property in 2022/23 was $2,054.92. This is an increase of 1.5 per cent when compared to the actual 2021/22 average rate of $2,023.67.  

The 2021/22 result was misstated due to the use of incorrect number of total assessments. The denominator used in 2021/22 was overstated by 667 properties (28,462 - 27,765). This resulted in an understatement of the average rate per assessment. The rate capping is consistent with the "Fair Go Rates" system. The forecast indicates that future rates revenue is in line with the forecast rate cap.

Description: Current assets compared to current liabilities
Variation:
Council had current assets in 2022/23 of $89.2 million (2021/22 $85.2 million) and current liabilities of $50.3 million (2021/22 $47.7 million). Working capital has remained in line with prior year.

Council remains able to meet liabilities as and when they fall due.

Description: Unrestricted cash compared to current liabilities
Variation:
The increase observed for 2022-23 is due to an increase in negative Unrestricted Cash, resulting from an increase in short term investments. 

The indicator excludes term deposits worth $55m from unrestricted cash, in which Council invests most of its funds to maximise returns.  
 
The amount of funds in term deposits are sufficient for Council to meet its obligations. 
 
In prior years, term deposits were included as part of unrestricted cash, resulting in significant variance when comparing the data.

Description: Loans and borrowings compared to rates
Variation:
Total debt as a percentage of rates for 2022/23 is 20 per cent, which is within Council’s Borrowing Policy.  
 
The increase in future years is due to planned borrowings for the delivery of key strategic infrastructure projects. This was approved as a part of budget finalisation process. The timing of drawdown will be subject to the delivery of projects.

Description: Loans and borrowings repayments compared to rates
Variation:
Council paid $8.2 million in principal and interest against its borrowings compared to $4.5 million in repayments in 2022/23. 
 
During 2022/23, Council borrowed $4 million to fund requirements. The result indicates Council’s ability to meet debt commitments from rate revenue. There are no principal repayments due for next two years.

Description: Non-current liabilities compared to own source revenue
Variation:
The increase in variance for 2022/23 when compared to the prior year is due to recognition of found assets worth $27.5 million as part of Council own-source revenue, though Council’s balance of non-current liabilities reduced in 2022-23.  
In its forecast Council is proposing to borrow new loans to fund capital works which results in the increment of this indicator in the future years. The ratio is still within the acceptable threshold.

Description: Asset renewal and upgrade compared to depreciation
Variation:
Depreciation expense increased by $3 million in 2022/23 due to $46 million worth of open space assets being added to Council's asset base.  
 
Due to the delays in capital projects, Council is expecting to carry forward a number of renewal expenditure projects to 23/24/ The delay of these project resulted in a reduced percentage of expenditure when compared to the depreciation in 2022/23.  
 
Future years renewal and upgrade expenditure is expected to increase compared to depreciation expenditure.

Description: Adjusted underlying surplus (or deficit)
Variation:
Financial year 2021/22 included Found assets realised as income for the amount of $27.5 million. This increment in income resulted in an abnormal surplus in previous financial year. 
During 2022/23, overall the income has increased and expenditure decreased compared to prior year apart from the variance due to found asset income realisation in prior year. Depreciation has jumped by $3 million, though its a non-cash expenditure, it contributes to an increased underlying deficit

Description: Rates compared to adjusted underlying revenue
Variation:
Financial year 2021/22 included found assets realised as income for the amount of $27.5 million, resulting in increased underlying revenue. This was an out-of-the-ordinary event. which suggests a decreased reliance on rates revenue as a primary source of revenue. 
The increase in variance for 2022/23 reflects Council’s genuine reliance on rates revenue as a primary source of income, and future years continue to show a similar pattern.

Description: Rates compared to property values
Variation:
Although rates income resulted in an increment of 6 per cent across the two financial years, property values have risen by 29 per cent. This has resulted in a higher denominator value, in turn resulting in the 16 per cent decrement in rates compared to property values.  
The gap between the regulated rate environment and market driven value continues to increase and is evident from the variance.

Description: Expenses per head of municipal population
Variation: 2022/23 expenses per head are in line with prior years. Last year experienced significant transfer of funds from capital to operating resulting in the exceptional increase observed in 2021/22.

Description: Infrastructure per head of municipal population
Variation:
A net revaluation decrease of $23 million in 2022/23 lead to reduced increment in the total carrying value of Infrastructure assets. This, combined with the increase in population, lead to the decrease in value per head across the two financial years. 

Last year, land values were not excluded from overall property, plant and infrastructure. This resulted in an overstated figure in 2021/22.

Description: Population density per length of road
Variation: Council manages a local road network of 1,828 km (2021/22 1,821 km), resulting in a ratio of 32 people for each kilometre of local road (2021/22 31)

Description: Own-source revenue per head of municipal population
Variation: The inclusion of open space asset recognition in 2021/22 resulted in a steep increase of revenue for the year. This was an extraordinary event, which resulted in a decrease in 2022/23.

Description: Recurrent grants per head of municipal population
Variation: Council's exit from Aged and Disability Services resulted in reduced grant funding received per head of municipal population.

Description: Relative Socio-Economic Disadvantage
Variation: The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) prepares an index of relative socio-economic disadvantage. The result for the municipality is six (where one is the most, and ten is the least disadvantaged).

Description: Percentage of staff turnover
Variation:
The increased turnover last year (41.9 per cent) was significantly influenced by the exit of Aged and Disability Services in response to sector Government funding changes. 

Council’s unplanned turnover rate decreased this financial year by 3.5 per cent, from 21.5 per cent in 2021/22 to 18.0 per cent for 2022/23.

Description: Health inspections of aquatic facilities
Variation: Bayside City Council does not operate aquatic facilities

Description: Utilisation of aquatic facilities
Variation: Council owns two aquatic facilities within the Bayside area: Sandringham Family Leisure Aquatic Centre and Middle Brighton Sea Baths.  Both these facilities are operated and managed under private commercial lease agreements.  Council is not responsible for the operation or management of the Sandringham Aquatic Centre and the Middle Brighton Sea Bath is not technically defined as an aquatic facility.

Description: Cost of aquatic facilities
Variation: Bayside City Council does not operate aquatic facilities

Description: Time taken to action animal management requests
Variation: Council continues focus on its responsiveness to animal management requests.  This is supported by proactive animal management patrols and activities. Officers continue to respond to complaints in a timely manner, at the low end of the range (under two days) consistent with comparable metropolitan councils.

Description: Animals reclaimed
Variation: The number of animals reclaimed is well above the average for metropolitan Councils due to a high proportion of animals collected being registered. Council takes a proactive approach to promoting responsible pet ownership, and a focus of reuniting pets with owners has contributed to this result.

Description: Animals rehomed
Variation: This rate of rehoming is similar to previous years, and while lower than the average for similar councils, it is partly because Bayside has a high percentage of animals reclaimed from Council by their owners, meaning that fewer animals need rehoming and demonstrating the high level of care by pet owners in Bayside including ensuring pets are registered.  The number of animals requiring rehoming has increased but the demand for rescue animals has reduced, with fewer being rehomed.

Description: Cost of animal management service per population
Variation: The cost of service is operating within budget and is in the middle of the range for metropolitan councils ($4-$17).

Description: Animal management prosecutions
Variation: Council conducts community education programs on responsible pet ownership to minimise breaches of the Domestic Animals Act. Despite the number of prosecutions doubling Council has maintained a 100% success rate on animal prosecutions through the Magistrate Court, as a result of good evidence and detailed briefs.

Description: Time taken to action food complaints
Variation: Cumulative time taken to action 49 food complaints Jan-Dec 2022 (calendar year) is 73 days  resulting in a reduced average to 1.49 days, which demonstrates a continued improvement as food businesses are now more accessible as trading conditions resume to pre-pandemic patterns of operation.

Description: Food safety assessments
Variation: All Class 1 and 2 premises that required an assessment were completed during the 2022 year.

Description: Cost of food safety service
Variation: Cost of the food safety service remains consistent with previous years. Salary costs are slightly reduced as the service carried a vacancy for a period of time.

Description: Critical and major non-compliance outcome notifications
Variation: Major and critical non compliances continue to be a high priority. Environmental Health Officers ensure that all major and critical issues identified during the assessment period are followed up as a priority within the required timeframe to mitigate the risk to the community.

Description: Council decisions made at meetings closed to the public
Variation: The number of decisions made at meetings closed to the public continues to be very low, however an increase of four decision from the previous year has resulted in a significant increase, as a direct result of a number of contractual matters being renegotiated due to the financial climate and contractor liquidation.

Description: Satisfaction with community consultation and engagement
Variation: The satisfaction survey undertaken in the reporting year was in person compared to the previous year which was conducted via a hybrid model (phone and in person). In person interviews may elicit a more engaged response. Furthermore, Council continues to improve and diversity its methods to engage with the community at all levels.

Description: Councillor attendance at council meetings
Variation: Councillor attendance at meetings during the reporting year had decreased compared to the previous year given some councillors took extended absence and were unable to be present at the meeting via electronic means.

Description: Cost of elected representation
Variation: The cost of elected representation has increased slightly compared to the previous year given the statutory increase in Councillor, Mayor and Deputy Mayor allowances though the increase was partly offset by a reduction in Councillor training during the reporting year.

Description: Satisfaction with council decisions
Variation: The satisfaction rating is sourced from the Annual Satisfaction Survey conducted by an independent research company.  The satisfaction survey undertaken in the reporting year was undertaken in person compared to the previous year in a hybrid model, this may have resulted in a minor increase in council decision satisfaction.

Description: Physical library collection usage
Variation: The library loans have continued to increase during this year, and has been complemented by new library collection stock. This is also supported by continued effort to build and maintain connection with active borrowers in the municipality (refer LB4).

Description: Recently purchased library collection
Variation: Following a cull of the library collection during pandemic closures, the collection has been reinvigorated with new stock.  This included specific collections that were targeted for renewal over the 2022-2023 period to meet demand.

Description: Active library borrowers in municipality
Variation: Bayside continues to connect with its borrowers through many streams including home deliveries, remote pickup, and installation of book lockers.  Since the pandemic libraries have extended opening hours providing more opportunities for active borrowers.  A slight decrease in the municipal population also drives a percentage increase.

Description: Cost of library service per population
Variation: Cost of the library service remains within the range, with a marginal increase that align with the increased participation and useage, and the return of all library branches to full operating hours.

Description: Infant enrolments in the MCH service
Variation: The number of birth notifications over the last five years has been trending downward (from 855 in 2018/19 to 729 in 2022/23). The percentage of infants enrolled in the service from birth notifications received remains within the target range. Council continued to deliver a very high level service with community satisfaction with the service in the excellent range.

Description: Cost of the MCH service
Variation: The maternal and child health (MCH) service provides support and information  to families with children aged from birth to school age who live within the municipality. The MCH cost has increased since last year. Reasons for the increase in cost are that with the end of pandemic declaration in October 2022 there was increased demand for staff leave, and increased casual backfill to cover planned leave to ensure continuity of service. There was also a significant increase in reactive building maintenance costs in the 2022/2023 year.

Description: Participation in the MCH service
Variation: Participation rates have increased compared to prior years. Monthly reminders for missed visits and a targeted program in conjunction with early childhood service providers helped to promote the MCH service and re-engage families with 2 and 3.5 year age visits, resulting in improved participation.

Description: Participation in the MCH service by Aboriginal children
Variation: Participation levels remains high based on a small number of families residing and enrolled in Bayside. Council has a strong commitment to close the gap and improve outcomes for first nations families.

Description: Participation in 4-week Key Age and Stage visit
Variation: Council's performance is consistent with the previous year. Council's services encourages newborns whose families are offered appointments for their two week and four week Key Age and Stage visits with the initial contact from the Maternal Child Health Service.

Description: Sealed local road requests
Variation: Significant rain events and flooding in late 2022 resulted in a spike in requests in that quarter, which have reduced significantly in the latter part of the year as issues have been addressed.

Description: Sealed local roads maintained to condition standards
Variation: The data is consistent with the previous year given Council's Pavement Management System and greater reliance on timely capture of actual conditions of roads.

Description: Cost of sealed local road reconstruction
Variation: Costs expended in 2022/23  are carried forward to 2023/24 reporting year as works are commenced but not yet completed. The project has been put on hold until 2025 to ensure alignment with works by utilities.

Description: Cost of sealed local road resealing

Description: Satisfaction with community consultation and engagement
Variation: In 2023, almost all councils that participated in the Victorian Local Government annual Community Satisfaction Survey (CSS) received lower overall performance index scores than in 2022. This trend is reflective across the state with almost all individual service areas and core measures declining significantly for the second consecutive year. Despite this trend, our overall performance is still performing significantly higher compared to the metro and state-wide levels. Our score in consultation and engagement is also significantly higher compared to the metro and state-wide levels. Further research was conducted last year to gain deeper insights into the factors affecting community perception of Council's performance in consultation and engagement. This investigation resulted in the identification of 14 quick wins, 9 of which have now been implemented. Some of these actions include promoting community awareness of consultation and engagement, employing clearer language in our communications, intensifying our focus on hyper-local issues during consultations, and enhancing our follow-up procedures after consultations to ensure that community voices are not only heard but also valued. Initial results indicate a higher level of community awareness and higher participation in consultation and engagement (excluding the December to February period).

Description: Health inspections of aquatic facilities
Variation: Brimbank City Council continues to conduct inspections of Council’s aquatic facilities during peak and off-peak periods. Description: Utilisation of aquatic facilities
Variation:
The Brimbank Aquatic and Wellness Centre (BAWC) opened on 12 September 2022. This resulted in a significant increase in visits to Brimbank aquatic centres as this facility proved very popular, particularly in the first four months of operation (warmer spring and summer months). Sunshine Leisure Centre also experienced a significant increase as there were no facility closures caused by COVID lockdowns, which had significantly impacted in prior years. 
Swim school member numbers also grew to over 4,500 across the two facilities by end of the financial year 2022-2023. BAWC achieved membership numbers of over 10,000 by the end of the calendar year (Dec 2022), with consistently high daily visitation numbers. This result is within the range expected by Council. Find out more about our leisure centres at https://www.brimbank.vic.gov.au/leisure-parks-and-facilities

Description: Cost of aquatic facilities
Variation:
The opening of the Brimbank Aquatic and Wellness Centre (BAWC) saw a significant increase in aquatic centre visitors and, hence, the income generated. This income, from the first year of BAWC operations, offset the annual aquatic centre investment, resulting in a substantial reduction in the cost per visit. 
The substantial decrease in cost per visit to aquatic centres is not anticipated to persist as a long-term trend. The introduction of the new facility initially sparked considerable community interest, but we expect this to level off over time. The cost per visit is currently outside the range expected by Council.  Find out more about our leisure centres at https://www.brimbank.vic.gov.au/leisure-parks-and-facilities

Description: Time taken to action animal management requests

The result is within the range expected by Council. Find out more about animal management at Brimbank http://www.brimbank.vic.gov.au/pets-and-animals.

Description: Animals reclaimed
Variation:
Brimbank City Council places a strong emphasis on responsible pet ownership and community safety. A primary objective of the Brimbank Domestic Animal Plan is to reduce the euthanasia rate of domestic pets. 
The Animal Management Service saw a significant increase ( 51%) in the number of animals collected by our animal management staff across the year. 2,093 animals were collected by Council in 2022/2023 compared to 1,394 in 2022/2021. The number of animals reclaimed is similar for both years, however this percentage remains low. Many Brimbank residents are experiencing financial difficulties and are unable to pay the costs of animal collection and longer term animal care. This result sits outside the range expected by Council. 
Find out more about animal management at Brimbank http://www.brimbank.vic.gov.au/pets-and-animals

Description: Animals rehomed

Many Brimbank residents are experiencing financial difficulties and are unable to pay the costs of animal adoption and longer term animal care.

Find out more about animal management at Brimbank http://www.brimbank.vic.gov.au/pets-and-animals

Variation: Successfully prosecuted all animal management cases referred to court.

Description: Time taken to action food complaints
Variation: Time taken to action food complaints has remained consistent with previous years.

Description: Food safety assessments
Variation: 100% of food premises received a mandatory inspection pursuant to the Food Act 1984 prior to renewal of registration.

Description: Cost of food safety service
Variation: The cost of food safety service remained consistent with previous year's results, and slightly below CPI increases.

Description: Critical and major non-compliance outcome notifications
Variation: Council's response to major-critical non-compliances has remained consistent in 2022/23, with a continued focus to ensure that staff actively respond to critical and major non-compliance notifications in a timely manner.

Description: Council decisions made at meetings closed to the public
Variation: The 2022/23 financial year saw a record capital works program which resulted in an increased number of confidential reports regarding the awarding of contracts during the reporting period.

Description: Satisfaction with community consultation and engagement
Variation: Feedback from community highlights a desire for targeted engagement, and that when feedback is sought, that Council communicates how this information was considered and influenced decisions. By June 2023, Council had undertaken a record number of 84 consultation and engagement activities, and saw a 52% increase in the number of people accessing Council's engagement platform.

Description: Councillor attendance at council meetings
Variation: There has been a reduction in Councillor attendance due to a combination of travel, illness and personal commitments among the Councillors. There were no Councillors on approved leave during 2022/23.

Description: Cost of elected representation
Variation: The variance is reflective of a reduction in legal and consultant costs compared to 2021/22.

Description: Satisfaction with council decisions
Variation: Feedback indicates some in the community want more information about local issues affecting their local areas and to see that their input has influenced Council decisions. This is consistent with feedback on satisfaction with community consultation and engagement. Providing more information about key issues and how community feedback has informed decision-making may improve satisfaction.

Description: Physical library collection usage
Variation: This increase is due to a full year of normal library services resuming from COVID, results from the 2019/20 through to the 2021/22 having been impacted by COVID restrictions and service closures.

Description: Recently purchased library collection
Variation: Slight increase on last year’s figure, mostly due to shipping schedules returning to normal. Council aims to maintain a collection target of 80% items purchased in the last 5 years.

Description: Active library borrowers in municipality
Variation: The total number of active library members for this year has increased on previous years. This indicator is an average of three years of active membership, therefore this measure still remains impacted by COVID. Active membership numbers are trending upwards towards pre-COVID levels.

Description: Cost of library service per population
Variation: Costs for last year were higher than usual due to the increased staff costs related to the reopening after covid lockdowns. This year’s figure is closer to the expected figure in a normal year of operating.

Description: Infant enrolments in the MCH service
Variation: This result is greater than 100% due to the number of babies where Hume City Council do not receive a birth notice, yet the baby is enrolled in the service following notification by domiciliary services and families contacting MCH to advise they have relocated to Hume on discharge from maternity services outside the Hume catchment.

Description: Cost of the MCH service
Variation: MCH cost of service reflects a resumption of full standard service delivery post-COVID and response to growing community and demand for MCH services and support in both Enhanced and Universal MCH services.  Recruitment to permanent vacant positions has also been achieved.

Description: Participation in the MCH service
Variation: MCH participation rates have remained steady with a slight increase despite COVID challenges and workforce pressures statewide. Hume continues to drive workforce planning and service innovations to address these challenges and maintain participation by the community in MCH services.

Description: Participation in the MCH service by Aboriginal children
Variation: MCH participation rates of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have continued to increase with targeted work to support engagement. Hume's Aboriginal Engagement Team continue to provide a multidisciplinary approach to support Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.

Description: Participation in 4-week Key Age and Stage visit
Variation: Participation rates and engagement in Maternal and Child Health Key Age and Stages visits has remained a key focus as MCH services have adapted innovatively in the recovery from COVID.

Description: Sealed local road requests
Variation: While there has been a significant increase in the number of requests, many of these requests relate to a small proportion of the overall network. A number of major State Government projects (Craigieburn Road and Sunbury Road upgrades and Gap Road level crossing removal) and associated road closures, plus a lack of arterial road capacity, and increased growth in the northern corridor have resulted in unforeseen deterioration to local roads. Furthermore, significant deterioration of the condition of many Council roads occurred due to a number of extreme weather events.

Description: Sealed local roads maintained to condition standards
Variation: Resurfacing work that has occurred through the year has ensured that the proportion of roads outside intervention levels has remained unchanged.

Description: Cost of sealed local road reconstruction
Variation: Urban road reconstruction is generally higher in cost/m2 as due to the requirements of thicker pavement, kerb & channel and other associated ancillary works to be constructed. The high variance is due to a higher proportion (97.5%) of rural roads being reconstructed in 2021/22.

Description: Cost of sealed local road resealing
Variation: Resealing program was a higher proportion of asphalt resurfacing compared to (2021/22) spray sealing/liquid roads, a greater number of roads requiring 100mm (thicker pavement) overlays. There was also an increase in asphalt unit price.

Description: Satisfaction with sealed local roads
Variation: Consistent with statewide results, there was a drop in satisfaction with local roads in 2022/23 - with Council's result being comparable to other interface councils. Wet weather conditions and number of significant storm events along with a number of State Government major road projects have impacted overall satisfaction of local roads and increases in sealed local road requests (see R1). The condition of sealed local roads is just one factor in this indicator result. Community members who provided a poor satisfaction rating with sealed local roads identified concerns about holes, cracks and uneven road surfaces, narrow streets and the impacts of heavy traffic and large vehicles on those streets.

Description: Time taken to decide planning applications
Variation: A number of long-standing applications have been completed and the accumulated days for these applications have increased the total processing days across all application types.  It is expected that this number will drop next year as the long-standing applications have now been substantially decreased.

Description: Planning applications decided within required time frames
Variation: The increased percentage demonstrates the effectiveness of the improvement projects which have been undertaken in the department across the last 12-24 months.

Description: Cost of statutory planning service
Variation: The slight increase is due to the lower number of new applications being received this financial year whilst staffing costs remain the same due to the permanent nature of the roles within the department.

Description: Council planning decisions upheld at VCAT
Variation: One Council decision has been upheld at VCAT in the last 12 months. Only seven applications were decided by VCAT over the reporting period out of an overall number of 939 planning decisions made by Hume. This represents a very small percentage of decisions and indicates that in general the vast majority of decisions being made by Council were in line with relevant planning considerations.

Description: Kerbside bin collection requests
Variation: Bin collection requests include missed bins, missing/stolen bins, complaints, and damaged bins. The reduction of requests during 2022/23 can be attributed to a reduction in missed bin requests.

Description: Kerbside collection bins missed
Variation: The decrease in 2022/23 can be attributed to improved levels of service delivery, including updating mapping and use of digital technology.

Description: Cost of kerbside garbage bin collection service
Variation: The increase in cost of kerbside garbage bin collection in 2022/23 is largely due to the increase in gate fees, predominately through an increase to the Victorian Government’s Waste Levy.

Description: Cost of kerbside recyclables collection service
Variation: The increase in costs of recyclables collection is a combination of increased costs in the delivery of the service and processing of materials in 2022/23.

Description: Kerbside collection waste diverted from landfill
Variation: The number of properties with Food and Garden Organics (FOGO) bins has continued to increase, this supports Hume City’s drive to divert away from landfill. However, over the 2022/23 year, there has been a decrease of tonnes of FOGO collected. Collected tonnage is very dependent on a variety of factors, including the weather, which can lead to subsequent changes in the diversion rate.

Description: Expenses per property assessment
Average rate per property assessment
Variation: The drop in the ratio is due to the expansion of new properties occurring later in the year. As a result, the rates income for these properties has been apportioned for the current year, rather than reflecting the full-year rates income.

Description: Current assets compared to current liabilities
Variation: The drop in the working capital ratio can be attributed to the increase in accrued expenditure, primarily driven by an influx of invoices received after June 30th, which are related to the 2022/23 financial year.

Description: Unrestricted cash compared to current liabilities
Variation:
As $325m of cash is in term deposit as at 30 June 2023 ($205m as at 30 June 2022) and the original term of those deposits is more than 90 days, hence, they are classified under other financial assets rather than cash balance. If include those term deposits, Council has over $394m cash and term deposits as at 30 June 2023. 

This ratio is expected to increase substantially in 2024 as the total cash and investments are aggregated for the purpose of the calculation and gradually reduces thereafter due to the substantial capital works program which is projected to result in a notable reduction in the cash balance.

Description: Loans and borrowings compared to rates
Variation: Council is currently debt free.

Description: Loans and borrowings repayments compared to rates
Variation: Council is currently debt free.

Description: Non-current liabilities compared to own source revenue
Variation: The primary reason for the surge is predominantly attributed to an increase in the non-current portion of the landfill provision subsequent to the revaluation undertaken in 2022/23. In the current provision, additional post-maintenance components relating to leachate and gas management have been included. These additions were required in order to comply with the rigorous standards established by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), thus driving the increase of the provision.

Description: Asset renewal and upgrade compared to depreciation
Variation: Following the organizational restructuring in 2022/23, the Council has allocated additional resources towards the delivery of the Capital Works program. This strategic decision led to a substantial 41% upsurge in capital expenditure on infrastructure projects, consequently influencing the ratio between asset renewal and upgrade in comparison to depreciation.

Description: Adjusted underlying surplus (or deficit)
Rates compared to adjusted underlying revenue
Variation:
This measure excludes items of a capital or non-recurrent nature including the non-monetary contributed assets, non-recurrent capital grants and capital cash contributions.

Adjusted underlying revenue is improving, primarily driven by an increase in operating grants received during 2022/23 compared to 2021/22. This growth is attributable to the advanced payment of the 2023/24 VGC grant in 2022/23, in addition to a new government grant allocated to support the free 3-year kinder program. Furthermore, more interest income has been realized due to increased term deposit rates and more user fees generated from the Leisure centre fitness and swimming program.

Description: Rates compared to property values
Variation: A full revaluation was undertaken and approved by Valuer-General Victoria in 2022/23, revealing an average of 5.48% increase in the property value across the municipality, consequently influencing the Rate effort ratio.

Infrastructure per head of municipal population
Variation: The rise in value is attributed to the substantial revaluation increase in infrastructure assets, assets contributed by developers, and investments in capital works.

Description: Population density per length of road
Variation: This measure remains consistent with previous years in line with population growth.

Description: Own-source revenue per head of municipal population
Variation: Own-source revenue grows at a faster pace than the population due to the predominant influence of the rise in interest income, increased user fee from the leisure centres and higher rates revenue from growth and rates cap increase.

Description: Recurrent grants per head of municipal population
Variation: The increase is primarily attributed to the advanced payment of the VGC grant funding received in 2022/23 and new grant received for the 3-year free kinder program.

Description: Relative Socio-Economic Disadvantage
Variation: This index score is a decile score and is calculated once every 5 years with the most recent being conducted during the COVID pandemic in 2021. This indicator combines census data from income, education, employment, occupation, housing and family structure. The COVID pandemic had a significant impact on the Hume community that resulted in an increase in disadvantage compared with the 2016 result.
