Description: Time taken to decide planning applications
Variation:
Council received 449 planning applications in the 2022/23 financial year and made 381 planning application decisions in the reporting period. with a median of 96 gross days. Gross days is the total number of days an application is with Council from the date of lodgement to the date of a decision. 

Unlike "statutory days" prescribed by planning legislation, gross days includes the period when Council waits for further information from permit applicants if additional information is required. Therefore, the number of gross days taken to determine an application is typically greater than statutory days in cases when further information is required.

Description: Planning applications decided within required time frames
Variation:
Of the 381 planning application decisions made, 199 applications were decided within 60 statutory days, and 24 VicSmart applications within 10 days. Statutory days relates to set timeframes identified by planning legislation during the planning application process. 

This includes a time period of 60 days which enables a permit applicant to lodge an application for review at the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) if Council exceeds this time period. Statutory days do not include the days when Council waits for further information from an applicant.

Variation: More library items were purchased this financial year but older stock has been left in the collection due to customer demand. Physical library use and borrowing rates have increased greatly which meant we were unable to remove as many older items as normal.

Description: Active library borrowers in municipality
Variation: Fall in active borrowers is less than the fall in municipal population. However, borrowers who are active are borrowing more items reflecting the increase in new stock and a refresh of the internal collection development policy which better reflects borrower needs.

Description: Cost of library service per population
Variation: The cost of the Library service decreased during lockdowns due to reduction in required staffing, including casuals. With libraries now fully operational, staffing budgets have increased.

Description: Infant enrolments in the MCH service
Variation: Small increase in enrolment numbers compared to birth notifications. This is due to clients transferring into the City of Monash post birth. The birth notification is sent from the birth hospital to the address the client provided. However, if the client chooses to reside with family in another municipality straight after birth, the history is transferred.

Description: Cost of the MCH service
Variation: Although the Maternal Child Health overall costs continues to increase each year, which is in line with the increase in the hourly MCH rate set by the Department of Health (this rate has increased from $123.25 in 2021/22 to $126.38 in 2022/23), the cost of Monash's MCH services slightly decreased this year when compared to the previous year, due to the reduced costs of cleaning as the service transitions back to universal cleaning precautions post COVID.

Description: Participation in the MCH service
Variation: Increase in participation in Maternal Child Health service. This is in response to the Department of Health COVID funding, which was used by the Monash Maternal and Child Health service to employ a Maternal and Child Health Nurse, on a contract. This nurse engaged with clients who missed their Key Age and Stage appointments during the pandemic. This funding was also used to increase capacity of the Maternal Child Health service to see clients for regular Key Age and Stage (KAS) visits. Outreach Maternal Child Health service to kindergartens and childcare centres also resumed offering alternative engagement methods to support working families.

Description: Participation in the MCH service by Aboriginal children
Variation: Participation in the Maternal Child Health service by Aboriginal children increased significantly this year (53 vs 43 in the previous year). Much work has been undertaken at the MCH centre level to create a culturally-safe and inviting space for all. This has included having culturally appropriate books, posters, toys, rugs etc within each office. The MCH staff continue to undertake cultural competency training. Staff are supported to ask all families if the wish to identify and have the knowledge to discuss, with family opportunities and supports available.

Description: Participation in 4-week Key Age and Stage visit
Variation: An increase in attendance at the 4-week Key Age and Stage appointment. This is likely due to all visits now having returned to the Maternal Child Health centre. A noted reduction in families reporting no longer being anxious about attending, when compared to attendance during COVID. Lessons learnt during COVID, such as telehealth appointments have also been used this year, which has further offered opportunities for families to engage with the Maternal Child Health service.

Description: Sealed local road requests
Variation: Number of sealed local road requests has remained steady as compared to previous reporting period. The number of requests is reflective of wetter conditions experienced during the last few years. Wet weather generally leads to a higher instance of issues such as potholes, therefore resulting in higher requests. City of Monash addresses such requests in line with intervention level, as per Council's Road Management Plan.

Description: Sealed local roads maintained to condition standards
Variation: Programming of road resurfacing has increasingly been better planned at Monash. Council has been utilising the predictive modelling within the Pavement Management System to prioritise roads to be resurfaced. Council’s continuous commitment to invest in the renewal of its road network has kept the number of roads classified as "very poor condition" to a low number.

Description: Cost of sealed local road reconstruction
Variation: There has been a small increase in the unit rate compared to 2020/21. There was no road reconstruction completed during 2021/22, therefore the price could not be compared against 2021/22. This change in price over two financial years is in line with the expectation, given there has been an increase in supply and labour costs.

Description: Cost of sealed local road resealing
Variation: The cost per square metre of road resealing has slightly decreased compared to 2021/22. The unit rate tends to fluctuate year on year based upon works undertaken on various road hierarchy types, such as minimum tonnages of asphalt placed on each road location, fluctuating petroleum price and the level of traffic management required. During the 2022/23 reporting period, Council was able to achieve a better pricing during the review of asphalt contract.

Description: Satisfaction with sealed local roads
Variation: The annual satisfaction with the Council's sealed local road has shown a notable improvement this year, with a rise from 72 to 75, an increment of 4%. This increase signifies a positive trend and reflects the Council's efforts in addressing road-related concerns and enhancing the overall road quality. It is encouraging to witness the community's growing satisfaction, which demonstrates the effectiveness of our ongoing initiatives. However, we must remain committed and ensure that this positive trajectory continues in the future. By maintaining our focus on road maintenance and implementing community-driven strategies, we can strive to provide an even better experience for our residents and reinforce their satisfaction with the sealed local road network.

Description: Time taken to decide planning applications
Variation: The time taken (gross days) to decide planning applications remains consistent with last year. It remains a good result with continuing improvement to process and procedures, including digitisation to allow the team to function at a high level.

Description: Planning applications decided within required time frames
Variation: A concerted effort has seen our decisions within 60 statutory days increase significantly as compared to last year, and is our best result as compared with the last four reporting years. This continues to be a focus for the team, who continue to attempt to balance decision timing against the quality of outcome. Fluctuating numbers (which have decreased since last year) and complexity of applications can affect this outcome.

Description: Cost of statutory planning service
Variation: The cost of service fluctuates year on year, with application numbers received being the key driver. With a decrease in application numbers and a drop in the number of major applications received, the cost of service has increased.

Description: Council planning decisions upheld at VCAT
Variation: There has been a drop in this statistic as shown in the table, more comparable to Council's 2022/23 result. Whilst this statistic is based on decisions made by VCAT within the specified period, as opposed to when applications were lodged, PPARS reporting (State Government) shows that a relatively small number of appeals against Council's decisions continue to be lodged at VCAT. In 2021/22, 65 appeals were lodged with VCAT against Council's decision with this reduced to 39 in 2022/23. This declining number of appeals lodged is pleasing. Council continues to make decisions consistent with its planning scheme and policies. VCAT decisions are reviewed and examined by officers to inform our decision making. However there are remaining applications where despite the  VCAT decision, Council maintains the form and type of development is inappropriate and cannot be supported by Council. We continue to see the trend of plans being substituted at VCAT rather than resolving issues at the application stage.

Description: Kerbside bin collection requests
Variation: There has been a continued increase in bin enquiries and requests due to the collection frequency changes in August 2022.

Description: Kerbside collection bins missed
Variation: Missed bin requests have increased this period due to resourcing issues in the waste industry. Note total lifts has also decreased since 2021/22 due to collection frequency switch.

Description: Cost of kerbside garbage bin collection service
Variation: The cost of the garbage collection service has decreased following the bin collection frequency switch in August 2022, due to garbage bins being collected fortnightly rather than weekly.

Description: Cost of kerbside recyclables collection service
Variation: Cost of recyclable bin collection has increased in line with an increase in contract costs.

Description: Kerbside collection waste diverted from landfill
Variation: The diversion rates from landfill have increased this period due to the diversion of food waste to compost, following the introduction of the Food Organics Garden Organics program and change in bin collection from weekly to fortnightly.

Description: Expenses per property assessment
Variation: Total expenses increased by 6.67% compared to 2021/22. Employee costs increased by 6.29%. The increase includes an additional 4.2FTE positions approved in the budget, temporary appointment of staffing resources and an increase in the Superannuation Guarantee Levy from the mandatory 10.0% to 10.5%. Material and Services increased across a number of expenditure areas mainly, waste management costs increased by $1.38M due to higher garbage collection and disposal costs in green waste due to the food organics, building and general maintenance by $0.8M to accommodate routine and reactive works that arose post pandemic restrictions and price escalations. Other expenditure items that increased include utilities costs by $1M due to all Council facilities resuming normal operations and general administration is higher by $1.24M due to increased program costs as services resume full activity. The efficiency trend is increasing as anticipated growth in expenditure levels are based on forecast CPI and wage growth, in addition to estimated growth in rates.

Description: Average rate per property assessment
Variation: The Minister for Local Government rate cap of 1.75% was applied to the 2022/23 rate charges.  This resulted in an increased ratio of 3.29% including an increase in property assessments. Future trends are indicating a steady improvement based on projected growth in rates.

Description: Current assets compared to current liabilities
Variation: The liquidity ratio decreased by 23% in 2022/23. Current assets are only higher by $1.3M but current liabilities increased by $18.96M. Creditor levels were higher by $15.11M than 021/22 levels due to a larger capital works program adopted for the 22/23 year.  In addition, trust funds and deposit ($1.46M) and unspent grants ($2.39M) have increased compared to the 2020/21 year. Council’s future forecast of working capital levels allow for significant development in the municipality which includes the major Suburban Rail Loop Authority (SRLA) project. Cash levels and potential property sales will impact working capital in the initial years which is expected to smooth to more consistent levels in outer years with a positive trend.

Description: Unrestricted cash compared to current liabilities
Variation: This ratio increased by 93% compared to 2021/22. The variation in this ratio reflects the level of cash held in short term deposits (with maturity dates of 90 Days or less) which is higher than 2021/22 levels. Higher current liabilities are mainly due to the capital works program expenditure which has increased Trades & Other Payables by $15.11M. Council has forecast cash levels to reduce given the planned capital works program for next year with a positive trend ratio to occur in future years.

Description: Loans and borrowings compared to rates
Variation: Council achieved a debt free status as at 30 June 2015. Future year budgets may require borrowings for various capital works projects but this will be considered and decided upon by Council at the appropriate time.

Description: Loans and borrowings repayments compared to rates
Variation: Council achieved a debt free status as at 30 June 2015. Future year budgets have included funding options for working capital depending on cashflow requirements which may be drawn down with the intention of repayment by financial year end. Allowance in forecasts have been included for this possibility. Borrowings for various capital works projects will be considered and decided upon by Council at the appropriate time.

Description: Non-current liabilities compared to own source revenue
Variation: The 2022/23 ratio compared to the prior year is slightly higher by 1.66%, whilst non-current liabilities have increased by $0.92M, the own source revenue in 2022/23 increased by 7.51%. Statutory Fees and Fines increased compared to 2021/22 with parking fines higher by $1.4M which is partly due to the previous year impacts of the COVID-19 lockdowns. User fees increased by $7.2M as leisure, aquatic and other Council facilities returned to full capacity. The trend is indicating a drop due to a forecast reduction in non-current obligations..

Description: Asset renewal and upgrade compared to depreciation
Variation: This ratio has increased by 36% on the prior year due to higher renewal and upgrade expenditure undertaken compared to asset depreciation. Council is still meeting its renewal targets and the 201.1% ratio confirms existing high level asset renewal and upgrade expenditure. This is forecast to continue into the next financial year with again another large capital works program expected. Outer years forecast more moderate levels of capital works expenditure.

Description: Adjusted underlying surplus (or deficit)
Variation: The 2022/23 adjusted underlying surplus ratio decreased by 144%. Despite recording higher revenue compared with 2021/22, expenditure increased by 6.67% due to higher employee costs, materials and services cost and depreciation have also contributed to a reduction in the adjusted underlying surplus in 2022/23.  Future years' projections are expected to improve with anticipated income levels and underlying results.

Description: Rates compared to adjusted underlying revenue
Variation: The trend reflects an increase in rate revenue by 2.7%, income from parking fines by $1.4M, which is partly due to the previous year impacts of the COVID-19 restrictions. User fees increased by $7.2M as leisure, aquatic and other Council facilities returned to full capacity, which has resulted in a ratio decrease to 66.06%. The future trend will be steady and in line with State Government projected increases in rates and charges.

Description: Rates compared to property values
Variation: The variance reflects Council’s overall rate revenue increase (2.7%) compared to the value of all properties in Monash which increased by an average 13.5% with the 2022/23 revaluation.  The trend is showing a steady increase based on State Government estimated increases in rates and charges and an average estimate on capital improved values as property value fluctuations are dependent on economic and market movement.

Description: Expenses per head of municipal population
Variation: The ratio has increased by 8.95% from 2021/22. Employee costs increased by 6.29%. The increase includes additional 4.2FTE positions, temporary appointment of staffing resources and increase in the Superannuation Guarantee Levy (SGL) from a mandatory 10.0% to 10.5%. Material and Services increased; Waste management costs increased by $1.38M, due to higher garbage collection and disposal costs in green waste due to the food organics initiative, Building and general maintenance increased by $0.8M to accommodate routine and reactive works that arose post pandemic restrictions, Utilities costs increased by $1M due to all Council facilities resuming normal operations and General Administration is higher by $1.24M due to increased program costs as services resume full activity. Population decreased by 1.68%.  A result of $1,092.72 again indicates Council is on the lower end of the expenses per head of municipal population.

Description: Infrastructure per head of municipal population
Variation: The increase of 11.38% primarily relates to a higher capital works expenditure program although municipal population decreased over the 12 month period by 1.68% impacting the final result.

Description: Population density per length of road
Variation: A slight decrease due to the decline in the municipal population. Although the trend has seen a reduction in recent years the longer-term expectation is a higher ratio as population numbers increase.

Description: Own-source revenue per head of municipal population
Variation: Own source revenue in 2022/23 increased by 7.51%. Statutory Fees and Fines increased compared to 2021/22. Income from parking fines increased by $1.4M, this is partly due to the previous year impacts of the COVID-19 restrictions. User fees increased by $7.2M as Council services and Leisure and aquatic facilities returned to full capacity. Municipal population decreased by 1.68% which has also contributed to the $921.50 result measure or 9.94% increase.

Description: Recurrent grants per head of municipal population
Variation: This ratio decreased by 3.13% over 2021/22 levels with an overall decrease in recurrent grant income of $0.32M. This is mainly due to reduction in General Home Care funding. Municipal population reduced by 1.68% which has also contributed to the $117.69 result.

Description: Relative Socio-Economic Disadvantage
Variation: The City of Monash is ranked in the top 10% on the SEIFA index, suggesting low levels of disadvantage.

Description: Percentage of staff turnover
Variation:
Council experienced 119 x terminations of permanent employees within 2022/23. This equates to 20 x less terminations than the previous financial year (2021/22).                                                                                                                           

Of our 119 x permanent terminations, 111 were voluntary (resignation or retirement). This represents a decrease of 11 x less voluntary terminations than the previous financial year. 

As the organisation has transitioned further into a post-COVID environment, turnover of permanent employees has reduced.

Description: Health inspections of aquatic facilities
Variation: Aquatic facilities were inspected once during the year, as required under section 3(1) of the Public Health and Wellbeing Act 2008.

Description: Utilisation of aquatic facilities
Variation: Utilisation of aquatic facilities increased significantly due to a return to stable opening hours following the pandemic-related closures combined with the first full financial year of attendance at the newly redeveloped Keilor East Leisure Centre (reopened in November 2021).

Description: Cost of aquatic facilities
Variation: Aquatic facilities returned an operating surplus for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic.  The financial performance of the Ascot Vale Leisure Centre and Keilor East Leisure Centre exceeded budget expectations which significantly reduced the cost of the service to the community. This was due to a strong return of patronage at the centres following pandemic-related closures.

Description: Time taken to action animal management requests
Variation: Council has concentrated effort and resourcing to improve task management, monitoring and follow-up which has resulted in significant service improvement.

Description: Animals reclaimed
Variation: Of the cats and dogs impounded, two thirds of dogs could be returned to their owners. A large proportion of impounded cats did not have owners to reunite with. The inability to reclaim cats in particular affects this service result. Through active promotion of animal registration, Council aims to improve the percentage of animals reclaimed.

Description: Animals rehomed
Variation: Of the cats and dogs abandoned and needing rehoming (ie. could not be reclaimed by owners), the majority were cats or kittens. Many of the cats and kittens that were deemed suitable were successfully rehomed.

Description: Cost of animal management service per population
Variation: Council increased its efforts to reduce animal abandonment and minimise the need for rehoming and reclaiming animals, through responsible pet ownership education. Activities such as increased patrolling of parks and public areas to proactively identify lost animals helped to ensure the timely return of animals.

Description: Animal management prosecutions
Variation: Council was successful in all animal management prosecutions. There was one prosecution.

Description: Time taken to action food complaints
Variation: Improved internal reporting and collaboration between delivery teams has resulted in quicker actioning of service requests.

Description: Food safety assessments
Variation: Improved record management has ensured that all relevant registered premises have received food safety assessments this financial year.

Description: Cost of food safety service
Variation: Improvements to food safety assessment processes resulted in a marked improvement in service delivery efficiency and effectiveness during 2022-23, with a minimal increase in the cost of the service.

Description: Critical and major non-compliance outcome notifications
Variation: Internal monitoring processes and improved record management resulted in Council following up on all non-compliance notifications through automated database alerts ensuring that all follow-ups are recorded and scheduled for action. There were 103 follow-ups made in 2022-23.

Description: Council decisions made at meetings closed to the public
Variation: While still low, there was an increase in decisions made at meetings closed to the public, done in accordance with section 66(2)(a) of the Local Government Act 2020. The increase is attributed to an increase in confidential reports relating to property matters.

Description: Satisfaction with community consultation and engagement
Variation: Council has made various attempts this year at improving opportunities for community to contribute to Council's planning in meaningful ways.  A Community Advisory Panel was established, a Community Carbon Emission Reduction Taskforce was activated and opportunities for residents to speak to Councillors through Neighbourhood Connect commenced.

Description: Councillor attendance at council meetings
Variation: With the introduction of a hybrid, in-person and virtual meeting setup, Councillors' attendance at Council meetings remained high.

Description: Cost of elected representation
Variation: The cost of governance service per Councillor remained steady. Costs included training and professional development, attendance at conferences and seminars, and other incidental expenses.

Description: Satisfaction with council decisions
Variation: Council remained committed to good communication and transparency about decisions made in the community's interest, evidenced via the live streaming of Council meetings and interactions with the community on a range of engagement platforms. The slight decline in satisfaction is representative of a trend occurring across local government generally.

Description: Physical library collection usage
Variation: Physical loans of library items continued to improve post pandemic-related closures. Library express locations and the mobile library van expanded the reach of library services for residents.

Description: Recently purchased library collection
Variation: The library collection continued to be renewed and updated consistent with previous years.  The increase in costs associated with collection development (cost of books and processing) has resulted in a smaller yield that can be achieved with the allocated budget compared to previous years.

Description: Active library borrowers in municipality
Variation: Active members continued to increase as the community returned to the library and restrictions associated with the pandemic were lifted. There was a significant increase in digital only membership.

Description: Cost of library service per population
Variation: Libraries are operating at full capacity, resulting in an increase in costs from the 2021-22 financial year.

Description: Infant enrolments in the MCH service
Variation: A higher number of deaths and stillbirths resulted in the number of infant enrolments being over 100%.

Description: Cost of the MCH service
Variation: Service costs increased slightly from 2021-22, reflecting greater use of casual staff to cover the increase in staff leave not fully utilised during the COVID-19 period of the previous financial year.

Description: Participation in the MCH service
Variation: The positive result reflects process improvement involving proactive appointment reminders.

Description: Participation in the MCH service by Aboriginal children
Variation: A small number of families identify as Aboriginal within the municipality (there were 27 known families requiring maternal and child health services). The result reflects a good participation rate in this population group.

Description: Participation in 4-week Key Age and Stage visit
Variation: The maternal and child health service consistently sees infants at the 4-week key age and stage visit. A small number of babies do not attend this visit due to factors including extended hospital stays, transfers to other municipalities and some families opting to see private midwives.

Description: Sealed local road requests
Variation: Council has been able to consistently respond to customer requests for sealed local roads.

Description: Sealed local roads maintained to condition standards
Variation: Council maintained all local roads to condition standards in accordance with the Road Management Plan. This was achieved through proactive inspections. Council’s standard requires all local roads rated as a Poor condition to be improved.

Description: Cost of sealed local road reconstruction
Variation: In accordance with the Road Asset Management Plan, ten streets were prioritised for reconstruction. Increased costs of construction materials and limited availability of contractors were the main factors affecting delivery of the service. The impact of these market conditions has resulted in an increase in cost per square metre which has limited the scope of work that could be delivered within the budget.

Description: Cost of sealed local road resealing
Variation: In accordance with the Road Asset Management Plan, five streets were prioritised for resealing. Increased costs of construction materials and limited availability of contractors were the main factors affecting delivery of the service. The impact of these market conditions has resulted in an increase in cost per square metre which has limited the scope of work that could be delivered within the budget.

Description: Satisfaction with sealed local roads
Variation: Council proactively inspects, maintains and renews its local road network in accordance with the Road Asset Management Plan and Road Management Plan schedules. Council will continue to refine its road reconstruction and resealing processes in the 2023-24 financial year to remain in line with community expectations.

Description: Time taken to decide planning applications
Variation: Improvements in processes and procedures reduced the number of days taken to decide planning applications.

Description: Planning applications decided within required time frames
Variation: Process improvements implemented in late 2021-22 have resulted in a significant increase in the number of applications decided within required timeframes across the 2022-23 financial year.

Description: Cost of statutory planning service
Variation: The number of applications received decreased year-on-year, while the cost of the service remained stable. Therefore the cost per application increased slightly from the 2021-22 year.

Description: Council planning decisions upheld at VCAT
Variation: The percentage of planning decisions upheld at VCAT increased year-on-year, reflecting appropriate assessment and decision making by Council. There were 12 VCAT Council decisions in relation to planning applications.

Description: Kerbside bin collection requests
Variation: The number of requests for collections increased year-on-year, primarily due to industry-wide driver shortages and inexperienced drivers. The waste contractor has focussed on the recruitment and training of drivers to improve service levels.

Description: Kerbside collection bins missed
Variation: A high rate of driver turn-over resulted in a shortage of experienced drivers, contributing to the high level of missed bin collections. The waste contractor has focussed on recruitment and training of drivers to address service levels.

Description: Cost of kerbside garbage bin collection service
Variation: Increased fuel and labour costs and increases in the landfill levy and disposal costs resulted in a 20 per cent increase in the lift rate (cost) per bin. In addition to these rising collection and disposal costs, the total tonnage of waste increased (by 3.5 per cent). Combined, these factors resulted in a higher cost of delivery of the service. Council is working on programs to divert waste from landfill through the rollout of a universal Food Organics Garden Organics (FOGO) service and waste reduction and recycling education campaigns.

Description: Cost of kerbside recyclables collection service
Variation: The cost of kerbside waste services increased by 20 per cent. This is due to an increase in fuel and disposal costs and a higher rate of contamination in recycle bins (which costs more to dispose of). There was a reduction in the total amount of recyclable material collected and disposed of in 2022-23 which offset some of the higher service costs.

Description: Kerbside collection waste diverted from landfill
Variation: There was less waste diverted from landfill, impacted by an increase in the rate of recycling material contaminated with waste material and needing to be disposed of at landfill, along with reductions in recycling and Food Organics Garden Organics (FOGO) waste. A recycling campaign will be activated to increase the education of residents around what can be recycled. Council will introduce a universal FOGO waste collection service in 2024 that will provide an additional 16,000 FOGO bins for residents. It is envisaged that these initiatives will help to reduce contamination and increase diversion from landfill.

Description: Expenses per property assessment
Variation: The increase is predominately due to Software as a Service costs (SaaS) related to the new 'Finance and Human Resource Systems implementation' Capital program being identified as operational in nature and therefore expensed accordingly as a one off. The anticipated increase in the number of property assessments in future years predicts a decrease in expenses per property.

Description: Average rate per property assessment
Variation: The variation is due to expenses related to Software as a Service (SaaS) increasing the costs per property in 2023. Major future development works influence the anticipated decrease in future years, due to the increase in the number of property assessments.

Description: Current assets compared to current liabilities
Variation: The increase is due to the reduction in current liabilities for unearned income from $18 million to $8 million. The increase in interest bearing loans and borrowings impacts the projected reduction in the indicator in future years.

Description: Unrestricted cash compared to current liabilities
Variation: The decrease is due to the investment of $39 million of unrestricted cash in term deposits with a maturity date greater than 90 days so the amount is presented in the balance sheet as Other Financial Assets. The predicted decrease in future years is due to the same reason where unrestricted cash is invested in term deposits with a maturity term greater than 90 days.

Description: Loans and borrowings compared to rates
Variation: The reduction is due to the repayment of $599K from the principal on the $10 million loan. An anticipated increase in the borrowing amount impacts the variance in future years.

Description: Loans and borrowings repayments compared to rates
Variation: The variation in 2022-23 is due to increase in the repayment on the principal balance of the $10 million loan. Anticipated increase of the borrowing amount effects the variance in future years.

Description: Non-current liabilities compared to own source revenue
Variation: The reduction in 2022-23 is due to an increase in own source revenue in user fees by $7 million and statutory fees and fines by $5 million. Anticipated increase of the borrowing amount impacts the increases in the forecasts.

Description: Asset renewal and upgrade compared to depreciation
Variation: The variance in 2022-23 is due to an increase in renewal spend from $8 million to $15 million. Predicted budgeted increase in renewal spend in the capital works program affects the forecast increases in the indicator.

Description: Adjusted underlying surplus (or deficit)
Variation: An anticipated decrease in externally funded operating grants affects the forecast for future years.

Description: Rates compared to adjusted underlying revenue
Variation: The variation is due to an increase in revenue in user fees and statutory fees and fines.

Description: Rates compared to property values
Variation: The variation is due to an increase in the property valuations from 2021-22 to 2022-23.

Description: Expenses per head of municipal population
Variation: The increase is predominately due to Software as a Service costs (SaaS)  related  to the new 'Finance and Human Resource Systems implementation' Capital program being identified as operational in nature and therefore expensed accordingly as a one off.

Description: Infrastructure per head of municipal population
Variation: The variation is due to the revaluation increase of Infrastructure Assets as at 30 June 2023.

Description: Population density per length of road
Variation: Population decline related to COVID-19 continued in 2022-23 which impacted on this result.

Description: Own-source revenue per head of municipal population
Variation: The variance is due to an increase in own source revenue in User Fees by $7 million and Statutory Fees and Fines by $5 million. A post COVID-19 recovery contributed to an increase in the utilisation of Council’s leisure facilities and a change to staff working hours in delivering the service resulted in an increase in the collection of infringement revenue.

Description: Recurrent grants per head of municipal population
Variation: The increase is predominately due to the transfer of unearned grants over the past three years from the balance sheet to recurring grants. This is a once off transfer.

Description: Relative Socio-Economic Disadvantage
Variation: The 2021 Census resulted in an unchanged rating for Socio-Economic Indexes for Areas (SEIFA). The rating remained high (a decile of 8 out  of 10) suggesting that there are more households with high incomes,  residents with educational qualifications and in highly skilled occupations  when compared to other Victorian local government areas.  When considered municipal-wide, the rating does not identify that there are localities within Moonee Valley that have higher levels of socio-economic disadvantage.

Description: Percentage of staff turnover
Variation: Year-on-year, the percentage of permanent staff resignations and terminations fell, returning to a rate comparable to turnover rates seen pre-pandemic, consistent with metropolitan councils generally.

Variation: Enhanced reporting functionality has allowed increased interrogation of data around requests resulting in more accurate appraisal of time taken to respond to animal requests.

Description: Animals reclaimed
Variation: With the continued efforts to promote responsible pet ownership including microchipping and registration this has enabled council to see a higher reclaim rate than in the previous year.

Description: Animals rehomed
Variation: With a higher return to home rate council has a lower rehoming rate as less animals are available for adoption due to returning home.

Variation: Council has not taken any cases to court in the 22/23 financial year.

Description: Time taken to action food complaints
Variation: The team still responded to food complaints within the expected range but had to shift their focus throughout the year for storm recovery and secondary impact assessments that needed to be conducted as part of emergency management and took priority over other requests.

Follow ups for remaining non-compliances will be conducted in the next financial year.

Description: Percentage of staff turnover
Variation: The decrease relates to the previous year containing a large number of redundancies, as Council exited the Aged and Disability service.

Description: Health inspections of aquatic facilities
Variation: Shire authorised officers carried out 12 inspections across Council’s three aquatic facilities: 6 at Yawa Aquatic Centre, 4 at Pelican Park Recreation Centre and 2 at Crib Point Pool. This includes 10 routine inspections and 2 investigation inspections

Description: Utilisation of aquatic facilities
Variation: The increase in the utilisation of our aquatic centres from 2021 is attributed to strong attendance numbers, an additional aquatic facility and four full trading quarters without any COVID closures, capacity restrictions, or significant facility maintenance/repair closures.

Description: Cost of aquatic facilities
Variation: The significant decrease in the costs of our aquatic facilities is mainly attributed to a 64% increase in total visitations compared to last year and Yawa Aquatic Centre performing beyond expectations, which meant that a significant amount of money was returned to Council through our profit share agreement with Belgravia Leisure. Additionally, the lump sum payments for both Pelican Park Recreation Centre and Crib Point Pool were reduced from November 2022 due to the start of the contract extension agreement with Belgravia Leisure.

Description: Time taken to action animal management requests
Variation: A 36% decrease in animal requests and a return to normal staffing levels have reduced the number of days to respond to requests. Last year COVID affected our staffing and our ability to respond to some animal matters over the 2021-22 year.

Description: Animals reclaimed
Variation: Despite collecting a similar number of animals as the previous year, fewer animals were reclaimed by their owners, which resulted in an overall decrease.

Description: Animals rehomed
Variation: Because there were fewer animals reclaimed by their owners this year, we were able to rehome more animals. In the event that animals cannot be reunited with their owners we always try our best to find them good homes.

Description: Cost of animal management service per population
Variation: The slight decrease in cost can largely be attributed to a decrease in administration costs, salaries/wages and overtime penalties across our local law enforcement and animal shelter teams. This is the result of staff shortages due to the continued impact of COVID-19.

Description: Animal management prosecutions
Variation: Council is committed to protecting the safety of the community and the health and safety of animals on the Peninsula by instituting prosecution only where appropriate and necessary. Council prosecuted 43 Animal Management matters over the year.

Description: Time taken to action food complaints
Variation: Despite a 41% increase in food complaints from the previous year, we have been able to decrease the time taken to action food complaints from 2022 due to improved data management and processes.

Description: Food safety assessments
Variation: The Shire continues to prioritise the community’s safety by ensuring that all food premises on the Peninsula receive an annual food safety assessment.

Description: Cost of food safety service
Variation: The decrease in the cost from 2022 is mainly due to a review of the resources budgeted against the food safety service to better reflect the actual cost of delivering this service to the community.

Description: Critical and major non-compliance outcome notifications
Variation: To ensure the safety of our community we continue to focus on food safety compliance programs across the Peninsula. Our critical and major notifications followed up result is largely consistent with the previous years, but slightly down from 2020.

Description: Council decisions made at meetings closed to the public
Variation: Nineteen decisions were made at meetings closed to the public. Of these, two related to Council business information that would prejudice the Council’s position in commercial negotiations if prematurely released; four were for legal privileged information, being information to which legal privilege or client legal privilege applies; eight were for personal information that if released would result in the unreasonable disclosure of information about any person or their personal affair and five included private commercial information (being information provided by a business, commercial or financial). Of the nineteen decisions, twelve decisions were released to the public following the meeting and only seven were retained as confidential items.

Description: Satisfaction with community consultation and engagement
Variation: Community satisfaction with Council consultation and engagement, conducted by an independent research company that measures the opinions of local people in the community, is on par with our 2022 result. We hope to address the decline from 2020 by improving how we consult and engage with our community to support their needs.

Description: Councillor attendance at council meetings
Variation: Councillor attendance has decreased slightly due to our move back to face-to-face meetings and a Councillor’s leave of absence, from 13 July to 27 November 2022, to contest the 2022 Victorian State Election.

Description: Cost of elected representation
Variation: Overall costs are significantly up from 2021 due to an increase in external consultants and catering expenses, which was driven by increase in physical Council meetings and events. An increase in Councillor workshops, training and development and Councillors claiming car milage as we emerge from a COVID-19 environment also contributed.

Description: Satisfaction with council decisions
Variation: Community satisfaction with Council decisions, conducted by an independent research company that measures the opinions of local people in the community, declined three index points from last year to 46. We hope to address the decline by better communicating our decision-making to the community.

Description: Physical library collection usage
Variation: The increase in our physical library usage can be attributed to a rise in the number of loans, which rose 47% against last year, the ongoing success of our book delivery service and participation in literacy programs such as Ready, Set, Read.

Description: Recently purchased library collection
Variation: The decrease from 2022 is primarily due to the ongoing impacts of COVID, which caused delays in the receipt of new material issues and an increase in the cost of transport as well as print and digital material. These all contributed to a decrease in the number of library collection items purchased compared to previous years.

Description: Active library borrowers in municipality
Variation: Whilst the activeness of our library borrowers increased slightly from 2022, the sum of our active library borrowers is still down 8% from 2021. This may be due in part to customer uncertainty in returning to public spaces because of concerns around COVID-19, which is of particular concern to our older-aged members.

Description: Cost of library service per population
Variation: The slight decrease from 2022 is largely due to the cessation of COVID-19 Marshals at each library's entrance, which was a requirement of the Victorian Government to ensure customer check-ins and vaccination status.

Description: Infant enrolments in the MCH service
Variation: The uptake of the service across the Mornington Peninsula remains high, demonstrating a high level of confidence in our maternal and child health services for families with children aged 0-6 years.

Description: Cost of the MCH service
Variation: The increase from 2022 is mainly due to changes in the administrative resources allocated to the Maternal Child Health service to better reflect the actual cost of service delivery, an increase in Universal casual salaries and wages due to permanent staff leave and increased costs associated with venue and equipment hire.

Description: Participation in the MCH service
Variation: Participation in the Maternal Child Health (MCH) service has remained consistent since 2020, with slightly higher results this year than in 2022. This is due to the reintroduction of the Preschool/Early learning centre program following COVID, where MCH nurses conduct Key Age and Stage consultations for children unable to attend a MCH centre.

Description: Participation in the MCH service by Aboriginal children
Variation: This year’s result saw a significant rise in participation from 2022. The rise is due to offering outreach services to childcare centres for Aboriginal families who cannot/do not want to attend a Maternal Child Health Centre, actively contacting clients who are overdue for a Key Age and Stage appointment and creating a welcoming and safe environment. 139 Aboriginal children attended the MCH service at least once in the year.

Description: Participation in 4-week Key Age and Stage visit
Variation: Participation has remained consistent over time with a slight dip in 2021, which demonstrates a high level of awareness and engagement with the Maternal Child Health service.

Description: Sealed local road requests
Variation: With the highest recorded spring rainfall in the past five years the number of sealed local road requests rose dramatically over the previous year.  As rainfall adversely affects road pavement, the amount of rain also made it difficult to fix potholes in a timely fashion as any rain heavier than a light sprinkle can ruin the hot-mix asphalt patch, which is a more cost effective and long-term fix than cold-patching asphalt repair. Reported defects decreased substantially in the second half of the year.

Description: Sealed local roads maintained to condition standards
Variation: Of the 1,392 kilometres of sealed local roads across the Shire, 1,348 kilometres were maintained within condition standards.

Description: Cost of sealed local road reconstruction
Variation: The decrease in the cost from 2022 reflects the minor local road works undertaken during the year. Last year, most of the work undertaken was on local arterial and collector roads, which require greater depths of asphalt and subsequently have a greater cost per square metre.

Description: Cost of sealed local road resealing
Variation: This year's increase is due to the works undertaken, in contrast to none undertaken in 2022 when resources were focused on the Shire's Road Rehabilitation program (sealed local road reconstruction).

Description: Satisfaction with sealed local roads
Variation: Community satisfaction with sealed local roads, conducted by an independent research company that measures the opinions of local people in the community, declined eleven index points from last year to 38. The decrease in our community’s satisfaction could be attributed to the highest recorded spring rainfall in the last five years, which resulted in an increase in sealed local road requests as rainfall adversely affects road pavement.

Description: Time taken to decide planning applications
Variation: We’ve been able to reduce the number of days taken with additional resources and process improvements, which have lowered application processing times.

Description: Planning applications decided within required time frames
Variation: Whilst we received fewer planning applications compared to the previous years, we were unable to increase our planning applications decided within timeframes result due to the backlog of applications, shortages in the labour market and an inability to fill vacancies, until recently.

Description: Cost of statutory planning service
Variation: The cost of the statutory planning service has increased and is comparable to pre-COVID results. During COVID, the cost of labour stayed the same or decreased due to labour shortages while the number of applications received was higher, which decreased the cost per application. The cost of the service is expected to stabilise and return to pre-COVID levels now that staff shortages have been addressed and if the number of applications remains stable or decreases.

Description: Council planning decisions upheld at VCAT
Variation: The increase in VCAT decisions upheld in comparison to 2021 is due in part to the emphasis on refined and informed decision-making across the planning unit, resulting in more easily defended decisions at VCAT. 48 VCAT decisions in relation to planning applications were made in the year.

Description: Kerbside bin collection requests
Variation: The decrease is primarily associated with a reduction of missed bin requests (rubbish), requests for a change in bin capacity (rubbish and recycling), stolen bins (rubbish) and damaged bins (rubbish and recycling).

Description: Kerbside collection bins missed
Variation: The decrease can be attributed to services returning to normal after the COVID-19 pandemic and the inclusion of additional service categories to ensure that partially emptied bins and bins that were not presented for collection, are not counted as missed bins.

Description: Cost of kerbside garbage bin collection service
Variation: A change to the contract rates for kerbside garbage bin collection and an increase in the landfill levy from $105.90 to $125.90 have increased the cost of our service.

Description: Cost of kerbside recyclables collection service
Variation: This year's increase reflects an annual adjustment to the rates for kerbside recycling bin collection and the introduction of a summer weekly recycling program, which was not offered last year.

Description: Kerbside collection waste diverted from landfill
Variation: The increase from last year is due to the increase in the number of residents opting into our Food Organics and Garden Organics service, which resulted in an increase in kerbside green/food waste and a reduction in household waste collected.

Description: Expenses per property assessment
Variation: Council always seeks to deliver the highest quality services in the most efficient way and has contained expenditure per property assessment through its goal for ongoing savings. The increase in 2023 are largely attributed to CPI, indexation of the Shire’s contracts and increased landfill capping provision.

Description: Average rate per property assessment
Variation: Council’s rates, our primary source of income that delivers essential services to our community, is limited by the rate cap, under the Fair Go Rates System, which was set at 1.75% for 2022/23. Increasing waste costs have also seen waste service charge increase 9% and supplementary income is 0.4% of the total rates revenue in 2023, which is growth of our rates income in 2023.

Description: Current assets compared to current liabilities
Variation: Increase in current assets due to higher cash and term deposits balances due to delayed expenditure for capital works and high interest rates, have increased our working capital.

Description: Unrestricted cash compared to current liabilities
Variation: The negative result has arisen as Council has allocated cash to term deposits in order to maximise the return on Council funds. The term deposits are reported as Other financial assets and total $100.5M at 30 June 2023. If the term deposits were considered as Cash and Cash equivalents then the Unrestricted cash ratio would have been +49.06%.

Description: Loans and borrowings compared to rates
Variation: No new loans drawn during the year and $4M principal loan re-payments as the rates revenue increase resulted this ratio to reduce.

Description: Loans and borrowings repayments compared to rates
Variation: Increase in rate revenue and paying-out of loans that expired resulted in the reduction in this ratio.

Description: Non-current liabilities compared to own source revenue
Variation: Own source revenue has increased by 5.1% due to rate revenue, increasing, higher usage of waste collection and disposal services and prepayment of the FY24 financial assistance grant. Non-current liabilities have remained stable, overall improving indebtedness ratio in 2023.

Description: Asset renewal and upgrade compared to depreciation
Variation: Asset renewal and upgrade are driven by the condition assessment of assets and varies year on year.

Description: Adjusted underlying surplus (or deficit)
Variation: This metric evaluates a council's capability to produce a surplus from its regular operations, excluding capital receipts. It's crucial for councils to generate adequate funds to maintain service levels in line with community demands. The decline can be attributed to the rise in the cost of services, which surpassed the council's revenue—primarily reliant on rate income. This ratio is vigilantly tracked in long-term financial planning to safeguard the Shire's capacity to offer essential services.

Description: Rates compared to adjusted underlying revenue
Variation: Although we have grown other revenue (own-source revenue) Council revenue is still largely dependent on rate revenue to fund services and capital works.

Description: Rates compared to property values
Variation: Property values continue to increase on the Mornington Peninsula and outgrows the rate cap.

Description: Expenses per head of municipal population
Variation: Council always seeks to deliver the highest quality services in the most efficient way and has contained expenditure per head of municipality through its goal for ongoing savings. The increase in 2023 is largely attributed to CPI, indexation of the Shire’s contracts and increased landfill capping provision.

Description: Infrastructure per head of municipal population
Variation: Investment in Infrastructure is impacted by the delivery of Capital Works Program ($42 million) and the revaluation of infrastructure assets.

Description: Population density per length of road
Variation: The population per density of local road resulted in a slight increase from last year to an increase in the 2022-23 municipal population.

Description: Own-source revenue per head of municipal population
Variation: Growth in own source revenue is in line with budget expectations and driven by the rate cap and supplementary rates during the year.

Description: Recurrent grants per head of municipal population
Variation: There is no material change in recurrent grants received in 2022-23 compared to prior year and a slight population increase resulting in a reduction of this indicator.

Description: Relative Socio-Economic Disadvantage
Variation: Mornington Peninsula's Relative Socio-Economic Disadvantage Index from the 2021 Census was in the eighth decile. The first decile indicates the most disadvantaged and the tenth decile indicates the least disadvantaged.

Description: Percentage of staff turnover
Variation: 69% of terminations for the FY23 financial year were related to resignations. This measure was impacted by the 2022 world-wide trend in increased turnover following the COVID-19 pandemic. This is reflected by 70% of these resignations occurring in the first half of the financial year, with voluntary turnover rates reducing from 10.4% in the first half of FY23 to 4.4% in the second half of FY23. Retirement rates continue to be steady at approximately 19% of total terminations.

Description: Health inspections of aquatic facilities
Variation: All pools were inspected and water quality tested during the financial year.

Description: Utilisation of aquatic facilities
Variation: Council has four outdoor seasonal pools open from December through to the second Monday in March. This season patron attendances were slightly down on the previous year due to cooler summer temperatures. Also, due to these cooler temperatures the pools were closed for 20 days, which affected attendances.

Description: Cost of aquatic facilities
Variation: This summer saw a 6% decrease in attendances than the previous year (20,767 in 2021/2022), while costs increased by 8%. This was mainly due to an additional cost of undertaking a pool shell integrity audit.

Description: Time taken to action animal management requests
Variation: All Animal Management requests are actioned within 1-2 business days.

Description: Animals reclaimed
Variation: There has been a 20% increase in animals reclaimed However, there has been a 193% increase in surrender of dogs by the public. This is due to the fact people bought dogs during Covid and now that most people have returned to the workplace they can no longer care for the dog/want the dog.

Description: Animals rehomed
Variation: Animals rehomed continued to improve.

Description: Cost of animal management service per population
Variation: An increase to permanent staff during 2022/2023 has increased employee costs.

Description: Animal management prosecutions
Variation: No animal prosecutions were undertaken for 2022/2023.

Description: Time taken to action food complaints
Variation: Internal staff shortages and changeover created disruption and setbacks compared to prior years performance and achievements.

Description: Food safety assessments
Variation: Internal staff shortages and changeover created disruption and setbacks compared to prior years performance and achievements.

Description: Cost of food safety service
Variation: While there has been an increase of 8% in the number of registered premises, there has been a 13% increase in the cost of providing the service compared to 2021/2022.

Description: Critical and major non-compliance outcome notifications
Variation: Similar to the improvement in 2021/2022, critical and major non-compliance follow-ups increased as inspection routines return to normal after several years of COVID-19 lockdowns.

Description: Council decisions made at meetings closed to the public
Variation: Three resolutions were passed at closed Council meetings.

Description: Satisfaction with community consultation and engagement
Variation: Council has worked hard to increase community consultation and engagement using a number of strategies including: media, briefings and streaming of Council Meetings on YouTube.

Description: Councillor attendance at council meetings
Variation: Two Councillors were absent on two separate occasions.

Description: Cost of elected representation
Variation: Service costs are returned back to pre-pandemic levels.

Description: Satisfaction with council decisions
Variation: Council has endeavoured to raise public awareness of its decisions, meetings, and activities through media releases, live streaming of Council Meetings to the internet, and actively encouraging community involvement in projects via our online community engagement platform.

Description: Physical library collection usage
Variation: In 2020/2021 the library was closed for 87 days during COVID-19 lockdowns, reducing the access of borrowers to the collection. For 2022/2023 loans have increased by 3% while collection items have decreased by 5%, compared to 2021/2022.

Description: Recently purchased library collection
Variation: No change in library collection items purchased.

Description: Active library borrowers in municipality
Variation: In 2020/2021 the library was closed for 87 days during COVID-19 lockdowns, reducing the ability of people to be active borrowers. Average borrower numbers over the last three years (2020/2021 to 2022/2023) have increased by 2% each year while average population over the last three years has only increased by 1%.

Description: Cost of library service per population
Variation: No change in cost of library services.

Description: Infant enrolments in the MCH service
Variation: All births were enrolled in the Maternal and Child Health service.

Description: Cost of the MCH service
Variation: MCH Enhanced services commenced in the 2019/2020 year but these costs were excluded from this indicator in error. If this service was included in the costs, the result adjusts to $76.30 for 2019/2020. There has been a 5% increase in service costs and a 2% decrease in MCH nurse hours worked compared to 2021/2022.

Description: Participation in the MCH service
Variation: Attendance decreased by 2.6% while enrolments remained stable.

Description: Participation in the MCH service by Aboriginal children
Variation: Low numbers of Aboriginal children (9 in 2019/2020, 15 in 2020/2021, 16.5 in 2021/2022, 19 in 2022/2023) can skew the percentage change between years.

Description: Participation in 4-week Key Age and Stage visit
Variation: Two children were born in June therefore not eligible for 4 week KAS visit.

Description: Sealed local road requests
Variation: The number of local road customer requests received in 2022/2023 increased by 17 from 2021/2022, but still remain low (total 32). The outcome could be the result of more defects being identified and repaired as a result of regular maintenance activities and council Road Management Plan inspections.

Description: Sealed local roads maintained to condition standards
Variation: The majority of sealed roads are in good condition, according to a recent survey of road conditions in 2020/2021.

Description: Cost of sealed local road reconstruction
Variation:
Road reconstruction unit rates vary depending on a variety of variables, including project value, specifications, the length, width, and depth of the road, material types, design criteria, and other related works, such as minor drainage, shoulders, cut/fill, and resource availability. Therefore, price fluctuation on road reconstruction projects is unavoidable for a rural council.

In comparison to the 2021/2022 financial year, the unit rate nearly doubled in 2022/2023. It might be the cause of the project's scope and the increased demand for civil contractors following the pandemic. However, the unit rate is within the targeted range.

Description: Cost of sealed local road resealing
Variation: Road resealing unit rates depend on a variety of parameters, including seal designs, road lengths, widths, aggregate sizes, material types, functionalities of the road, associated preparation work, resources on hand, etc. Therefore, a rural council cannot avoid price fluctuations for road resealing projects. Due to the aforementioned factors, the unit rate was slightly raised from 2021/2022 to 2022/2023. However, the unit rate falls within the targeted range.

Description: Satisfaction with sealed local roads
Variation: There was a slight decline in customer satisfaction reported in the 2022/2023 survey, but overall, there haven't been any significant changes in the way the council provides services. The recent flood events may have contributed to the drop in satisfaction, but the council is still making great efforts to restore the roads to their pre-flood conditions.

Description: Time taken to decide planning applications
Variation: Higher staff turnover resulted in delays on planning decisions compared to 2022/2021.

Description: Planning applications decided within required time frames
Variation: Significant change in staffing arrangements impacted decision timeframes

Description: Cost of statutory planning service
Variation: Legal costs increased by 150% in 2022/2023 with a number of complex VCAT issues that required legal representation, compared to 2021/2022. In addition, employee costs increased by 38% due to higher than average staff turnover.

Description: Council planning decisions upheld at VCAT
Variation: There were five VCAT decisions during this reporting period, with four being upheld by VCAT. Numbers of appeals made to VCAT were three in 2021/2022 and four in 2020/2021.

Description: Kerbside bin collection requests
Variation: Kerbside bin collection requests increased slightly compared to 2021/2022.

Description: Kerbside collection bins missed
Variation: Increased number of rural households with a kerbside waste/ recycling service can cause occasional collection issues

Description: Cost of kerbside garbage bin collection service
Variation: There has been a 6% increase in the costs of processing general waste compared to 2021/2022.

Description: Cost of kerbside recyclables collection service
Variation: There has been a 1% decrease in the costs of processing recyclables compared to 2021/2022.

Description: Kerbside collection waste diverted from landfill
Variation: Kerbside collection waste diverted from landfill has improved by 2.75% compared to 2021/2022.

Description: Expenses per property assessment
Variation:
Expenses in 2021/2022 were higher than usual mainly due to the increase in the provision for landfill liability to reflect the estimated costs associated with cell capping at the Castlemaine landfill. With the cell capping works completed in 2022/2023 expenses have decreased by 4%. 
Forecast results expect an average increase of 1%.

Description: Average rate per property assessment
Variation:
Increase is in line with the Fair go Rate System (FGRS). 
Forecast results are conservatively averaging 2.2% rate caps, with property assessment numbers expected to remain stable.

Description: Current assets compared to current liabilities
Variation: Current liabilities decreased by 32% at 30 June 2023 with the completion of cell capping works (paid from the landfill provision) at the Castlemaine landfill. In comparison current assets increased by 3%. The ratio increases in forecast years to reflect the reduction in loan borrowings as existing loans are paid off.

Description: Unrestricted cash compared to current liabilities
Variation:
An error was identified in calculating unrestricted cash in prior years and results should have been 2019/2020 +27.02%, 2020/2021 -15.94% and 2021/2022 -47.03%.
Council’s term deposits are invested for periods of up to twelve months and these funds are not included in the calculation of unrestricted cash. If these funds were included, Council’s unrestricted cash ratio would be 106.21% for 2022/2023. 
Carried forward capital works and conditional grants unspent are unknown and not considered for unrestricted cash in future years.

Description: Loans and borrowings compared to rates
Variation: No new loans occurred during the year, while principal repayments were made across the year that reduced the level of borrowings. No new loans have currently been budgeted for.

Description: Loans and borrowings repayments compared to rates
Variation: One loan was paid off during 2019/2020 year. Two loans were paid off during 2021/2022 year, including one that required a $1M balloon repayment, and two loans were paid off and no new loans were drawn down in 2022/2023 year. No new loans have currently been budgeted for.

Description: Non-current liabilities compared to own source revenue
Variation: Non-current liabilities decreased from June 2022 to June 2023 due to the decreased non-current provision for landfill rehabilitation costs as capping of the Castlemaine landfill was completed in May 2023. The continuation with declining own source revenue growth is expected in forecast years due to rate capping while non current liabilities are reducing with borrowings being paid off.

Description: Asset renewal and upgrade compared to depreciation
Variation: $7.4M of renewal works were completed. during 2022/2023 and $3.4M of new capital works was also completed. Forecast years focus more on completing renewal works and some upgrade works with the indicator returning to above 100% in 2023/2024.

Description: Adjusted underlying surplus (or deficit)
Variation: Overall, income was 29% greater than budget, while expenses were 5% greater than budget. In terms of income, the 2023/2024 Federal Assistance Grants was paid early in 2022/2023 ($6.3M), an unbudgeted amount of $933k was recognised for a reduction in the expected future cost of landfill rehabilitation works, interest income was greater than budget by $703k, and contributions, both monetary and non-monetary, were greater than budget by $1.22 million.

Description: Rates compared to adjusted underlying revenue
Variation: Total rate revenue (including waste charges) increased by 2.7%. The adjusted underlying revenue increased by 13.7% in 2022/2023, due to an increase in operating grants received. This increase in grants is not expected to continue in forecast years.

Description: Rates compared to property values
Variation: Capital improved values (CIV) have increased at a greater rate than rates revenue and is expected to continue in forecast years.

Description: Expenses per head of municipal population
Variation: Expenses in 2021/2022 were higher than usual mainly due to the increase in the provision for landfill liability to reflect the estimated costs associated with cell capping at the Castlemaine landfill. With the cell capping works completed in 2022/2023 expenses have decreased by 4%.

Description: Utilisation of aquatic facilities
Variation:
The combined number of visits recorded at Wellington Shire Council's indoor and outdoor aquatic facilities during 2022/23 was 235,569. 
This equates to an average of 5.15 aquatic facility visits per Wellington Shire resident for the year.

Description: Cost of aquatic facilities
Variation: During 2022/23, Wellington Shire Council's indoor and outdoor aquatic facilities operated at a cost to Council of $ 1,840,441 and recorded 235,569 visitors, which resulted in an average cost per visitation of $7.81. While the operation of Council's aquatic facilities both indoor (Aqua Energy) and outdoor (Sale, Maffra, Heyfield, Yarram & Rosedale) were impacted by significant increased utilities and maintenance costs (increase of 46% in total across all facilities) the growth in visitation reduced the overall cost of aquatic facilities compared to other years. Attendances returned to pre-covid levels, with outdoor pools and learn to swim participation particularly well attended.

Description: Time taken to action animal management requests
Variation: Local Laws officers responded to 1,371 domestic animal management requests during the 2022-23 financial year, with an average initial response time of 1.12 days. Animal management requests included lost, wandering or nuisance pets, animal welfare concerns, dog attack reports, reports of dangerous/menacing dogs and reports of illegal pet breeding activities.

Description: Animals reclaimed
Variation: 626 domestic animals were collected by Council's Local Laws officers during the 2022-23 financial year, 421 were reunited with their owners. Unclaimed animals are placed into the care of Victorian Animal Aid Trust and if suitable, rehomed through their pet adoption program.

Description: Animals rehomed
Variation: Through the dedicated work of Victorian Animal Aid Trust, 157 unclaimed animals were rehomed during the 2022-23 financial year, in addition to 421 lost animals returned to their owners.

Description: Cost of animal management service per population
Variation: Direct animal management costs for the reporting period have been calculated at $917,368 with a cost per head of population of $20.05. This figure is slightly higher than last year due to continuing increases in general costs.

Description: Animal management prosecutions
Variation:
9 successful animal management prosecutions were finalised during the 2022-23 financial year. 
Prosecutions included serious dog attacks, unregistered breeders and prevention of cruelty to animal matters.

Description: Time taken to action food complaints
Variation: Council received a total of 10 food complaints in 2022 which is one less than 2021. This demonstrates that community members are aware they can report concerns about the safety or handling of food that is sold within Wellington Shire via Council's Customer Action Request system. To minimise any further risk to the community, Council is committed to responding to food safety complaints as a priority. This is demonstrated by the 2022 results once again showing all food safety related complaints were responded to within 1 day.

Description: Food safety assessments
Variation: For the year ending 31 December 2022, 27 premises required a food safety assessment with 24 food safety assessments being undertaken. The high inspection rate demonstrates that Council has prioritised the conduct of these inspections. There were 3 new premises registered late within the reporting period, therefore these food safety assessments were prioritised for the following registration period. During 2022, the legislative requirement relating to food safety assessments changed.  As a result, the number of premises requiring food safety assessments is significantly lower in 2022 compared to other years.

Description: Cost of food safety service
Variation: Direct cost of Council's food safety program per all registered and notifiable food premises is $418.12. The cost of delivering food safety service has remained steady during the last couple of years.

Description: Critical and major non-compliance outcome notifications
Variation: For the 2022 calendar year, there were 27 non-compliance notifications. All 27 food premises received one or more follow up inspections to ensure compliance with the Food Act 1984.

Description: Council decisions made at meetings closed to the public
Variation: Council made 228 resolutions during the 2022/23 financial year. Of those decisions, only 10 or 4.39% were made in meetings closed to the public. Council maintains transparent processes in order that the community is informed by and engaged with Council business. Additionally, all meetings open to the public are broadcast live via Council's website and made available via an online video archive. Council actively strives to make few decisions in closed session to ensure transparency and accountability to the community in its decision making.

Description: Satisfaction with community consultation and engagement

Description: Councillor attendance at council meetings

With the extension of the Ministerial Good Practice Guideline for Virtual Meetings, Council continues to embrace a hybrid Council meeting model, combining in person and virtual attendance. This flexibility has allowed Councillors to continue to effectively participate in Council meetings while balancing a return to in person Councillor engagements across the shire.
